messages.body_plain:
Cooper, (list)

To augment what Chris said: in terms of modelling detectability, there are 3
options:

1. Fit a global detection function (assumes same detection prob across all
sites).  To do this in Distance, you have site as a stratum, and ask for density
estimates and encounter rate by stratum in the model definition | estimate tab,
but detection function global.

2. Fit a separate detection function to each site.  To do this you have the same
setup as above, except a different model definition where you tick the box in
model definition | estimate for detection function by stratum.

3. Do multiple covariate distance sampling, where you have site as a covariate
(or some other biologically meaningful variable such as canopy cover).  This is
a nice halfway house between 1 and 2.  For more on this, see the following
paper, which is available from my web site.
Marques, T.A., L. Thomas, S.G. Fancy and S.T. Buckland. 2007. Improving
estimates of bird density using multiple covariate distance sampling. The Auk
127: 1229-1243.

The above choice is essentially a model selection question, and you can use AIC
to choose among the options. Again, see the above paper, and also the distance
sampling books and Distance manual.

Hope this helps,

  - Len

On 27/01/2012 23:57, Chris Merkord wrote:
> > Hi Cooper,
> >
> > ESW is just the strip width multiplied by the estimated detection
> > probability, so if you have a lot of variation in ESW it is probably
> > because your estimated detection functions vary considerably.  If there is
> > no reason to suspect that the true detection function varies between sites,
> > then the question is why your estimated detection functions vary so much.
> >   I'm guessing its because of small sample sizes.  Again, if there is no
> > reason to suspect that the true detection function varies between
> > sites, then perhaps you should consider pooling detections across sites to
> > estimate your detection function. You can still get site-specific density
> > estimates.
> >
> > Cheers,
> >

messages.body_plain:
A follow-up answer to Jeff's:

I agree that distance sampling is not a panacea!  For some rare species, =
for=20
example, you need a survey that's specifically targeted for that species,=
 and=20
can't hope to get a good estimate as part of some larger multi-species su=
rvey.

Since you are trying to do something with Distance:

- You could try analyzing the data for the rarer bird jointly with some m=
ore=20
common bird(s) that seem comparable, with species as a covariate in the=20
detection function, perhaps.  A paper on this is:
Alldredge, M. W., K. H. Pollock, T. R. Simons, and S. A. Shriner. 2007.=20
Multiple-species analysis of point count data: A more parsimonious modell=
ing=20
framework. Journal of Applied Ecology 44:281=96290.

- For species where detectability of the more common species is best mode=
lled as=20
constant over sites (see my previous post for how to find this out), you =
can use=20
a multiplier in Distance to take detection function from the common speci=
es and=20
apply to the rare one -- see the Distance help on multipliers.

- You may want to consider model selection uncertainty.  An example with =
a rare=20
species is here (paper on my web site):
Williams, R. and L. Thomas. 2009. Cost-effective abundance estimation of =
rare=20
marine animals: small-boat surveys for killer whales in British Columbia,=
=20
Canada. Biological Conservation 142: 1542-1547.

- There is no rule of thumb for minimum sample size that I like.  The few=
er=20
samples you have, the less well you can detect violations of assumptions =
and=20
other problems.  However, if the true detection function has a very wide=20
shoulder, then very few distances are needed to do a good job of fitting =
it.  I=20
think the intro book says 60-80 for line transects is a good number -- bu=
t in=20
the above paper I think we had 18.

Hope this helps,

  - Len

--=20

messages.body_plain:
Hi
I did exactly the same, on more or less the same species in French Guiana. =
The Detection function is, in most of the cases, not different between hunt=
ed in non hunted sites. I think that the density of the forest is the stron=
ger constraint so that the fleeing distances does not vary so much (animals=
 escape more rapidly in hunted places, but not from so much longer distance=
s , I think) So just test before if the detection fonctions are not the sam=
e in your case, so that you can pool the data across sites to get the ESW, =
and then get a site by site dentity. I agree that it will never be enough f=
or some very rare species, but it will be usefull for all the common ones.
Carlos Peres also tested that between-sites variance in PD are not greater =
than the within sites (ANOVA), before pooling the perp distances .
Sincerely.

bjet=A0: generating robust estimates for rare species (hunted vs. non-hunte=
d tropical forest)

Hello all,

     I have a follow-up question to one I posed earlier.  I completed a tra=
nsect study of primates and large frugivorous birds across three tropical f=
orest sites in Peru.  The sites are under varying degrees of hunting pressu=
re, with one intact site, one moderate site, and one highly impacted site. =
 My survey effort at each site was just over 100km, and the Distance analys=
is was done on a site-by-site basis, with no pooling or stratification.  Gi=
ven that some of my target species occur at very low densities as a result =
of hunting pressures, the data and resulting Distance analysis is not very =
robust.  I have a few questions in response to this:

1.  How does one generate a robust density estimate for a species which is =
so rarely encountered?  My understanding is that pooling the data for a giv=
en species across all three sites would be inappropriate in this case, as t=
he detectability of that species is not the same across sites (the animals =
at a hunted site will respond by avoiding surveyors and fleeing more quickl=
y and quietly, thus they will be less detectable than at an intact site, wh=
ich will skew the estimates).

2.  It seems that generating a good density estimate of a rarely encountere=
d species would require an astronomical amount of survey effort.  Is there =
a consensus guideline for the minimum recommended effort?  I have read that=
 40 observations is a good general minimum, but that is an unreasonable goa=
l for a rare species...

3.  If after 10 weeks of intensive field study, I am not able to generate e=
nough data for a robust density estimate of a rarely encountered species, h=
ow useful is Distance as a conservation tool for assessing populations of r=
are species?

     I have read through the Distance Sampling book and several additional =
publications guiding the sampling of tropical forest primates, but I am not=
 able to find specific answers to these questions.  I would appreciate any =
feedback or suggestions on how to proceed with my analysis.  If you have qu=
estions in response to my post, I would be happy to elaborate. If this is a=
 recurring question among the Distance community, I would gladly compile th=
e responses to this post to share.  Thanks very much for your time!!  Since=
rely,

Cooper Rosin
cooper...@duke.edu
Masters of Environmental Management Candidate Duke University

messages.body_plain:
Hi List,

I'm analysizing ship-based seabird transect data where the distances were
collected in a small number of distance bins (4 or 5). With such a small
number of bins, there is often not enough degrees of freedom for a
Chi-square goodness of fit test on the "Detection Fct/Global/Chi-sq GOF
test" page of the results. I seem to remember being told at the DS course a
few years ago that, in such cases, a useful rule thumb for guidance is that
if the sum of the numbers in the "Chi-square values" column exceeds the
number of distance bins, then the fit is probably poor. Or was it that none
of the individual values should exceed 1?

Does this sound familiar to anyone - or did I make the whole thing up?

Thanks,
Dave

--

messages.body_plain:
Dave:

I don't think either of these ideas sound familiar, they are not part of
our standard discussion of chi-square tests.  In your first case (sum of
chi-square greater than or equal to number of bins): when the test
statistic equals the degrees of freedom p=0.50, so your describing a
situation where test statistic equals df+1 which might not be strong
evidence to suggest poor fit.  Second rule (no chi-sq component exceeds
1) this will place you close to the result of your first rule which
would also provide some support for the fit of the model in question.

messages.body_plain:
Dave, I'm not sure what the issue is.  What do you mean by 'too few' df?  Y=
ou only need 1df to get a valid chi-sq goodness-of-fit test.  If you have l=
ots of detections, that test should have reasonable power for detecting goo=
dness-of-fit.  If you have 0 df, then you should get a perfect fit because =
you have fitted the maximum number of parameters possible.  A more likely p=
roblem is that you have too few detections, so that the chi-sq goodness-of-=
fit test has low power.  In that case, if your distance data are not groupe=
d, you still have the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises tests, though=
 their power isn't likely to be a whole lot better.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Hi Steve,

Thanks for the reply. Here's an example that I think illustrate what I mean.

We have 2089 detections with distances collected in 4 intervals (0-50,
50-100, 100-200, 200-300 metres). Since our distance data are grouped, the
KS and CvM tests are not an option.

I am fitting a half normal key function with automatic selection of simple
polynomial adjustments:

Model  3
    Half-normal key, k(y) = Exp(-y**2/(2*A(1)**2))
    Simple polynomial adjustments of order(s) :  4, 6
       Results:
       Convergence was achieved with   36 function evaluations.
       Final Ln(likelihood) value =  -2894.8067
       Akaike information criterion =   5795.6133
       Bayesian information criterion =   5812.5469
       AICc =   5795.6250
       Final parameter values:   105.98892     -1.4968388      18.497826
      ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity.
**

    Likelihood ratio test between models  2 and  3
       Likelihood ratio test value    =    64.5628
       Probability of a greater value =   0.000000
 *** Model  3 selected over model  2 based on minimum AIC

Here's the output from the "Detection Fct/Global/Chi-sq GOF test" results
page:

  Cell           Cut           Observed     Expected   Chi-square
   i            Points          Values       Values       Values
 -----------------------------------------------------------------
   1     0.000        50.0          611      584.44        1.207
   2      50.0        100.          466      469.76        0.030
   3      100.        200.          484      566.54       12.026
   4      200.        300.          528      468.26        7.621
 -----------------------------------------------------------------

 No Degrees of Freedom for the test. No test possible.

In this case, no Chi-square test was possible due to having too few distance
intervals or equivalently too many parameters in the model, right?

I'd still like to be able to judge the fit of this model. I know I can
visually examine the detection probability plot, but what I'm wondering is,
in general, can I infer anything from the "Chi-square Values" column in the
table, even though no test was possible?

Thanks!

Dave

--
Dave Fifield
da...@mun.ca

From: Stephen Buckland [mailto:st...@st-andrews.ac.uk]

To: Dave Fifield; DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
Subject: RE: [DIST-SAMP] Goodness of fit assessment with insufficient
degrees of freedom

Dave, I'm not sure what the issue is.  What do you mean by 'too few' df?

You only need 1df to get a valid chi-sq goodness-of-fit test.  If you have
lots of detections, that test should have reasonable power for detecting
goodness-of-fit.  If you have 0 df, then you should get a perfect fit
because you have fitted the maximum number of parameters possible.  A more
likely problem is that you have too few detections, so that the chi-sq
goodness-of-fit test has low power.  In that case, if your distance data are
not grouped, you still have the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises
tests, though their power isn't likely to be a whole lot better.

Steve Buckland
